recorded.outcome:q-parallel-errors: Option c. Lines 65-67: 'A local that refers to an object is private, but the object is shared once a second thread can reach it: through a field, a collection, an argument passed to another thread, or a task given to an executor.' Lines 59-61: 'the value copied is a reference, and both copies point to the same array on the heap'. Reference table: 'the object a local refers to | yes, once a second thread has the reference'. The page never mentions parallel streams or says ArrayList is not thread-safe; the reader must carry the int[] lost-update result (lines 49-62) over to a shared ArrayList. The stem's 'runs the lambda on several threads' closes the stream gap, so the decision holds.

recorded.outcome:q-report-locale: Option c. Lines 197-198 (javadoc: the child receives initial values 'when a child thread is created'); lines 219-221: 'A ThreadPoolExecutor creates its threads as tasks arrive, inside submit, on the submitting thread. acme's request created the mailer's only thread, which copied acme and keeps it for every later task.' Summary line 317-318. The page shows only a one-thread pool. Extending this to four threads made by four requests needs the stem's 'submitted while others were still running' (it makes sure four distinct threads exist), and the page does not state that rule itself.

recorded.outcome:q-slot-counters: Option a. Lines 244-246: 'Coherence works on cache lines, not on variables ... two cores writing different variables in one line pass the line back and forth.' On 'fewer in total than one worker': lines 281-282 and 288 show two threads on adjacent fields doing 200M increments in 2,224 ms against one thread doing 100M in 495 ms, so the pair's total throughput was below one thread's.

recorded.outcome:q-parallel-errors:a: Refuted by lines 65-66 (the referenced object is shared once a second thread reaches it) and the Reference row 'the object a local refers to | yes'. The premise is partly true: the local itself is unshared (lines 13-15).

recorded.outcome:q-parallel-errors:b: Refuted by lines 59-60: 'the value copied is a reference, and both copies point to the same array on the heap'; Summary line 312: 'a copied reference still points to a shared object'.
recorded.prompt:q-parallel-errors:d: the page and the question, and nothing else
recorded.pass:q-parallel-errors:d: independent readers: a page-free reader (wording only) and a page reader with the page and the quiz, each a fresh agent
recorded.outcome:q-parallel-errors:d: Partly true: the verdict 'unsafe' is right and frames are per-thread (line 62 'each thread has its own frame'). The reason is refuted by lines 58-59: the lambda copies the captured local when it is created, so the other threads never read the caller's frame. The page states this capture-copy rule but does not say outright that this is why other threads need no access to the caller's frame.

recorded.outcome:q-ready-loop:a: Refuted by lines 77-79: 'caches are coherent: a coherence protocol makes every core that reads an address see the latest store that has reached any cache', and by lines 119-120 (not from a cache).
recorded.prompt:q-ready-loop:b: the page and the question, and nothing else
recorded.pass:q-ready-loop:b: independent readers: a page-free reader (wording only) and a page reader with the page and the quiz, each a fresh agent
recorded.outcome:q-ready-loop:b: Refuted by the experiment: the writer does a plain write in both cases (lines 84-85, 101) and the opaque reader saw it within ~111-134 us, with no fence on the writer side. Coherence (lines 77-79) also means a value in the writer's cache is visible to readers. The page never says outright that 'plain writes need no fence to leave the core'; the reader has to infer it from the experiment.

recorded.outcome:q-ready-loop:d: Refuted by lines 123-125: the store buffer 'holds a write briefly before it reaches the cache', and by the opaque result (a plain write with no fence seen in microseconds). The page does not say explicitly that a store buffer drains without a fence; 'briefly' carries that.

recorded.outcome:q-slot-counters:d: Refuted by lines 300-301: 'A line that is only read can sit in every core's cache at once; a write takes it from all of them.' Partly true: every update does read the field that holds the array, but a line that is only read does not contend. Nuance: the page's own header-line finding (lines 291-295) shows that reads which share a line with written data do suffer. The array's header and length sit next to its first slots, so this point bites the array object, not the reference field option d names. The option still fails as stated.
